purpose: Show the inspect, debug, measure, fix and verify loop that every DevTools task follows.
explanation: You start on the live page. You inspect the element or log in Elements and Console. You pause the code with a breakpoint in Sources. You measure the cost in Network, Performance or Memory. You try a fix as a live edit or a local override, then reload to verify it.
alt: Flowchart: Live page, then Inspect with Elements and Console, then Debug with Sources breakpoints, then Measure with Network, Performance and Memory, then Edit live or use local overrides, then Reload and verify, which loops back to the live page.

learning_check.question: Which panel do you open after a breakpoint shows the code is correct but the page is still slow?
learning_check.answer: A measuring panel: Performance for slow scripts or rendering, Network for slow requests, Memory for growing memory.

title: The DevTools inspect, debug, measure and fix loop
Finding a leak with two heap snapshots
purpose: Learn the order of steps that finds an object that stays in memory and the reference that holds it.
explanation: Take a snapshot, do a suspect action, undo it a few times, and take a second snapshot. Compare the two, pick an object that was added, and read its Retainers to find the reference that keeps it alive.
alt: Flowchart of eight steps: Snapshot 1, do suspect action, undo it a few times, Snapshot 2, Comparison view, select added object, read Retainers, clear the reference.

learning_check.question: Which section shows what keeps a selected object alive?
learning_check.answer: The Retainers section, which lists the objects that point to it.

title: Request timing phases in the Network Timing tab
purpose: Learn the order of the phases a request passes through, so you can name the slow one.
explanation: A request waits in the queue, may stall, resolves the server address, connects, sends the request, waits for the first byte, then downloads the body. The slow phase tells you whether to fix the network, the server or the payload.
alt: Flowchart of seven phases in order: Queueing, Stalled, DNS Lookup, Initial connection, Request sent, Waiting for first byte (TTFB), and Content Download. The widest bar shows where the request lost time.

learning_check.question: Which phase is long when the server is slow to build the response?
learning_check.answer: Waiting (TTFB), which includes one round trip plus the server's preparation time.

title: How a source map turns generated code positions into original positions
purpose: Show the order of steps from a generated file to an original source position.
explanation: The generated file points to a map file. The tool fetches the JSON and splits the mappings string into lines and segments. It decodes each segment from base64 VLQ and adds the numbers to the previous values. The result is an original file, line and column.
alt: Flowchart with seven steps: the generated file ends with a sourceMappingURL comment, the tool fetches the map JSON, splits mappings on semicolons into lines, splits each line on commas into segments, decodes VLQ fields, adds them to the previous values, and gets an original file, line and column.

learning_check.question: Why must a tool decode segments in order instead of reading one segment alone?
learning_check.answer: Most fields are relative to the previous segment, so each value depends on the ones before it.

title: Connecting desktop Firefox DevTools to a phone over USB
purpose: Learn the order of steps that attach desktop DevTools to a tab on an Android phone.
explanation: You switch on USB debugging on the phone and in Firefox for Android, plug in the cable, and refresh devices in about:debugging. After you authorize the computer on the phone, the device and its open tabs appear. Inspect attaches DevTools to the tab.
alt: Flowchart of seven steps: enable Developer options and USB debugging on the phone, enable Remote Debugging via USB in Firefox for Android, connect the cable with adb installed, Refresh devices in about:debugging, authorize the computer on the phone, see the device with its tabs, click Inspect.

learning_check.question: What must you do on the phone after you click Refresh devices?
learning_check.answer: Authorize the computer, so the device then appears with its open tabs.

title: Lighthouse module map
purpose: See which part of Lighthouse records a page load, which computes metrics, which scores, and which packages it.
explanation: Gather records a trace and a devtools log. Metrics parses them and computes LCP and TBT. Audits and scoring turn the numbers into a result. Build bundles the same code for the CLI and for DevTools.
alt: Flowchart: Gather feeds Metrics, Metrics feeds Audits and scoring, and Build connects with dotted lines to Gather and to Audits and scoring.

learning_check.question: Which module never calls an audit?
learning_check.answer: Gather. It only records the trace and the devtools log; audits read them later.

title: Lighthouse flow from page load to score
purpose: Follow one page load from recording to a 0 to 1 audit score.
explanation: The navigation runner connects, starts the gatherers, loads the page and stops them. The runner gives each audit only its required artifacts. The audit asks for a metric, then the scoring code averages the scores.
alt: Sequence diagram: navigationGather connects a Driver and runs gatherers, the Runner passes artifacts to an Audit, the Audit asks a metric artifact for a value, and ReportScoring scores categories.

learning_check.question: Where do recording and judging meet?
learning_check.answer: In the saved artifacts: the trace and devtools log that gather produces and audits consume.

title: DevTools frontend: four studied modules
purpose: See which parts of the DevTools frontend own the protocol, source maps, HAR and heap snapshots.
explanation: The protocol client carries every command and event between DevTools and the browser. Heap snapshots arrive as protocol chunks. Source maps are fetched through the page loader. HAR files are built from the request model.
alt: Flowchart of four modules: cdp-client sends commands and events to the browser and passes heap profiler chunks to heap-snapshot; source-map loads maps through the page loader; har reads the request model filled from network events.

learning_check.question: Which module carries heap snapshot chunks from the browser?
learning_check.answer: The cdp-client module, which delivers HeapProfiler events to the heap-snapshot code.

title: A heap snapshot request across the protocol client
purpose: Follow one numbered command and its unnumbered events from the model to the worker.
explanation: The model sends a numbered command. Chunk events arrive without a number and are routed by session to the model, then the proxy passes them to a worker. The reply with the same number finishes the stored promise.
alt: Sequence diagram: HeapProfilerModel sends takeHeapSnapshot with an id through the connection and transport; chunk events return, are routed by session to the model and forwarded through the proxy to the worker; the reply with the same id resolves the promise.

learning_check.question: How does the connection tell a reply from an event?
learning_check.answer: A reply carries an id that matches a stored promise; an event has only a method.

title: Finding a leak with two heap snapshots
purpose: Find a leaked object by comparing two heap snapshots and reading its retainer path.
explanation: Do the action and then undo it before the second snapshot. Anything still added after the undo is a leak candidate, and the Retainers section names the reference that keeps it alive.
alt: In the Memory panel you take a heap snapshot, do a suspect action and undo it a few times, then take a second snapshot. The Comparison view lists objects that were added and are still alive. You select one, read its Retainers to see which reference keeps it alive, and clear that reference. A detached DOM node is the common case: it is removed from the page, but JavaScript still points to it.

learning_check.question: You remove a list from the page, but the second snapshot still shows a Detached ul. Where do you look to find what keeps it alive?
learning_check.answer: In the Retainers section of the selected object: it lists the objects that point to it, for example a JavaScript variable that still holds the list.

title: From matching rules to one computed value
purpose: Show why the Styles pane lists many rules for one property while the Computed pane shows one value.
explanation: Several CSS rules can match one element. The Styles pane lists every matching rule and marks the overridden declarations. The cascade picks one winner for each property. The Computed pane shows only that applied value, and its box model diagram shows the final margin, border, padding and content size.
alt: Flowchart: matching CSS rules go to the Styles pane, which lists all of them, and to the cascade, which picks a winner. The winner goes to the Computed pane, which feeds the box model diagram. Conclusion: read Styles for why, Computed for what applies.

learning_check.question: A button's color is wrong. Which pane tells you the value the browser actually uses, and which tells you which rule lost?
learning_check.answer: The Computed pane shows the applied value. The Styles pane shows all matching rules, with the overridden declarations marked, so you see which rule lost.

title: Read one request in the network waterfall
purpose: Name each timing phase of a request and say which phase grows when the network, the server or the queue is slow.
explanation: A long part of a waterfall bar points to the step that lost time: Waiting points at the server or the round trip, Content Download at payload size or network speed, Queueing at competing requests.
alt: The Network panel draws each request as a bar in the Waterfall column. The Timing tab splits the bar into Queueing, Stalled, DNS Lookup, Initial connection, Request sent, Waiting (TTFB) and Content Download. Waiting is one round trip plus server time. With Slow 4G throttling, Waiting and Content Download grow. When six connections to one HTTP/1.1 origin are open, a seventh request grows its Queueing bar. The Initiator and Priority columns say why and how urgently a request ran. A HAR export saves the session and leaves out Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers by default. The bar lengths in this walkthrough are example values, not measurements.

learning_check.question: A request has a long Waiting (TTFB) bar and a short Content Download bar. Which part of the exchange is most likely slow?
learning_check.answer: The server or the round trip, because Waiting is one round trip of latency plus the time the server needs to prepare the response.

learning_check.question: You switch the Throttling menu from No throttling to Slow 4G and reload. Which bars grow the most?
learning_check.answer: Waiting (TTFB) and Content Download. Waiting is one round trip of latency plus server time, and Content Download depends on network speed. A slower network makes the round trip and the body transfer slower, so both bars grow.

title: From a recorded trace to a faster interaction
purpose: Learn the order of steps that finds a long task in a trace and checks that a fix brings INP under 200 ms.
explanation: Throttle the CPU, record a trace while you click, and read the Main track. A task over 50 ms is a long task. If the interaction takes over 200 ms, split the work so the page can paint first, then record again.
alt: Flowchart: set CPU throttling, record and click, read the Main track flame chart, decide if a task is over 50 ms; if yes it is a long task, the interaction over 200 ms is flagged, split the work and record again until INP is at or under 200 ms; if no, check the Layout shifts track for CLS at or under 0.1.

learning_check.question: Which part of a 300 ms task does the Performance panel shade red?
learning_check.answer: The last 250 ms, the part over 50 ms.

title: Pausing on the stale search response
purpose: Show the search race and the conditional breakpoint pause as one static diagram for readers without JavaScript.
explanation: The search box calls onInput for re and then for react. Both calls await a fetch on line 5. The react response arrives first, and the re response arrives late, so render on line 6 shows stale results. A conditional breakpoint on line 6 with q !== input.value pauses only on the late response. At that pause the Call Stack shows the await separator and the onInput call that started the wait; the ignore list hides library frames (Chrome DevTools docs, breakpoints and JavaScript debugging reference; ECMA-426 ignoreList).
alt: Sequence diagram: the search box sends re then react to onInput, which fetches both from the server. The react results return first and the re results return late. On line 6 the condition q !== input.value is false for react and true for re, which pauses with q re and input.value react; the Call Stack shows onInput line 6, await, onInput line 5.

learning_check.question: Why does the conditional breakpoint pause only once?
learning_check.answer: Only the late re response has a q that differs from the current input value react.

title: A search race in the Sources panel
purpose: See why a slow response can overwrite a newer one, and which parts of the Sources panel help you catch it.
explanation: A race bug depends on timing, so you must stop the code at the right moment. Breakpoints pause it there; Scope and the Call Stack then show the values and the callers.
alt: A search box sends a request for re and then for react. The react response arrives first and the late re response renders last, so the list shows the wrong results. The Sources panel has a Navigator, an Editor and a Debugger with the Breakpoints, Scope and Call Stack panes. A breakpoint pauses the page; a logpoint prints to the Console and does not pause.

learning_check.question: What is the difference between a breakpoint and a logpoint?
learning_check.answer: A breakpoint pauses the page so you can read Scope and the Call Stack. A logpoint prints a message in the Console and does not pause.

title: Catching the search race with breakpoints
purpose: Use a line breakpoint, a conditional breakpoint, a logpoint and the ignore list on line 6 of the search code, and read the async call stack at the pause.
explanation: The async part of the Call Stack, below the await separator, shows the call that started the wait. Its Scope still holds the old q, so you see that a stale response reached render.
alt: Line 6 calls render(items) after await search(q). A line breakpoint there pauses twice: first with q react, then with q re, which leaves the wrong list. A conditional breakpoint with q !== input.value pauses only on the stale re response. At that pause the Call Stack shows onInput line 6, an await separator, and onInput line 5 with two vendor frames below. A logpoint prints the same values in the Console without pausing. Adding vendor/events.js to the ignore list hides the two vendor frames.

learning_check.question: At the conditional pause, q is re and input.value is react. What does that tell you?
learning_check.answer: This response belongs to an older request. render is about to replace the newer react results with stale re results.

title: Pick the breakpoint for the bug
purpose: Connect each kind of bug to the breakpoint type that catches it, and recall what to read when the page pauses.
explanation: Each breakpoint type answers a different question. Choose the one that pauses closest to the cause, then read the state at that moment.
alt: Use a line-of-code breakpoint when you know the line, a conditional breakpoint when only some calls are wrong, and a logpoint when you must not pause. title: Why a click can feel slow
purpose: See how a busy main thread delays the next paint after a click, and how the Performance panel records it.
explanation: The main thread runs one task at a time, so a long task holds back the paint that answers a click.
alt: An intro to the Performance panel: Live metrics show LCP, CLS and INP for the open page, a recorded trace shows every task on the main thread, and a long task between a click and the next paint makes the interaction slow.

learning_check.question: What does the Performance panel show before you record anything?
learning_check.answer: Live metrics: your local LCP and CLS at once, and INP after you interact with the page.

learning_check.question: The click handler task lasts 300 ms. Which part does the Performance panel shade red?

title: Which Console utility reads which part of the page
purpose: Show that each Console utility is a shortcut to one part of the live page state.
explanation: The Console runs JavaScript against the live page. Each utility reads one part of it: $0 is the element selected in Elements, $$() returns an array of elements that match a selector, getEventListeners() returns the listeners on an object, and copy() puts a value on the clipboard. A live expression pins one expression to the top of the Console and refreshes its result.
alt: Diagram: the Console prompt points to five targets. $0 leads to the selected element, $$(selector) to an element array, getEventListeners to event listeners, copy() to the clipboard, and a live expression to a pinned value. Conclusion: pick the utility by the page state you need.

learning_check.question: You need every product card on the page as an array. Which utility do you type?
learning_check.answer: $$('.card') with the card selector. It returns an array of all matching elements, unlike $0, which is only the selected element.

title: Which browser tool fits which debugging task
purpose: Show that you pick a second browser by the task: Firefox for layout and fonts, Safari for bugs that only Safari shows.
explanation: Each arrow starts at a debugging task and ends at the tool that shows it best. Firefox draws a grid or flex overlay on the page and gives each variable font axis its own slider. Safari Web Inspector is the tool for a bug that only Safari shows; you open it from the Develop menu. Chrome DevTools stays your default for everything else.
alt: Diagram with three task-to-tool arrows. Grid or flex sizing leads to the Firefox Layout tab, variable font axes lead to the Firefox Fonts tab, and a Safari-only bug leads to Safari Web Inspector through the Develop menu. Conclusion: choose the browser by the task, not by habit.

learning_check.question: A flex item renders 40px narrower than you expect. Which tool explains its final size?
learning_check.answer: The Firefox flexbox inspector in the Layout tab. It shows the item's Content Size, Flexibility, Minimum Size when clamped, and Final Size.

title: The retainer path that keeps a detached list alive
purpose: See why a node that left the page still uses memory: a chain of references from a GC root still reaches it.
explanation: The code removed the ul from the document tree, but the global variable detachedTree still points to it. The path GC roots, Window, detachedTree reaches the ul and its ten li children, so the garbage collector cannot free them. The Retainers section of a heap snapshot shows this path. Set detachedTree to null and the path breaks.
alt: Flowchart: GC roots point to the Window global, Window points through the variable detachedTree to a detached ul, the ul points to ten li nodes, and a dashed line shows the ul was removed from the document tree, so the reference from detachedTree alone keeps eleven nodes in memory.

learning_check.question: Which single reference must you remove so the garbage collector can free the ul and its ten li children?
learning_check.answer: The global variable detachedTree. It is the only link from a GC root to the detached ul.

title: How desktop DevTools reach a tab on a phone
purpose: Show that each phone browser pairs with one desktop entry point, and that the phone must allow debugging first.
explanation: Each row is one connection path. Desktop Chrome opens chrome://inspect and reaches Chrome on an Android phone with USB debugging on. Desktop Firefox opens about:debugging and reaches Firefox for Android the same way. Desktop Safari lists an iPhone in its Develop menu over a cable or an Xcode wireless pairing. The desktop tools then inspect the real tab on the phone.
alt: Diagram with three connection paths. chrome://inspect connects over USB debugging to an Android Chrome tab. about:debugging connects over USB debugging to a Firefox Android tab. The Safari Develop menu connects by cable or Xcode pairing to an iPhone Safari tab. Conclusion: pick the desktop browser that matches the phone browser.

learning_check.question: A bug appears only in Safari on an iPhone. Which desktop entry point do you open?
learning_check.answer: The Develop menu in desktop Safari on a Mac, after you turn on Web Inspector on the iPhone and show developer features on the Mac.

title: One paused position traced back through a source map
purpose: See how DevTools turns a position in a minified bundle into a file and line in the original source.
explanation: DevTools follows the sourceMappingURL link and fetches the map. It finds the segment for the generated line, decodes its VLQ letters into changes, and adds them to the previous segment. The result is an original file, line and column, counted from 0. The example string AACD follows ECMA-426 Sections 6, 9.2 and 11.
alt: Flowchart from left to right: paused in app.min.js on the second line, follow sourceMappingURL to fetch the map, take segment AACD, decode it into the changes 0, 0, +1 and -1, add them to the previous values, and land on sources 0, line 1, column 0, so the Sources panel shows the authored file.

learning_check.question: The previous segment ended at source 0, line 0, column 1. The next segment decodes to 0, 0, +1, -1. Where does it point?
learning_check.answer: Source 0, line 1, column 0 (counted from 0), because each field is added to the previous value.

title: Where the page keeps state: storage areas and the service worker
purpose: Place each storage area that the Application panel shows, and the service worker between the page and the network.
explanation: The page has two paths for state. A request passes through the service worker before it reaches the network; the Network panel shows this as the Request to ServiceWorker phase. Saved values live in Cookies, IndexedDB or Cache storage, the three areas of the Application panel's Storage section. Stale state hides in either path.
alt: Flowchart: the page sends a request to the service worker, which sends it on to the network; the page also saves state into a group labeled Application Storage that holds Cookies, IndexedDB and Cache storage, so old state can come from the worker path or from storage.

learning_check.question: A tester sees old JavaScript after a deploy, but the server sends the new file. Which two places in the Application panel do you check first?
learning_check.answer: Service workers and Cache storage, because the worker sits between the page and the network and can answer with a saved response.

title: Source map stack resolver: execution flow
purpose: Show how a minified stack frame becomes an original file and line in the mini project.
explanation: main.ts reads the stack and the map. decodeMappings splits the mappings string and calls decodeVlq for each segment. resolveFrame calls originalPositionFor to find the original file and line. formatStack hides frames from ignoreList files.
alt: Flowchart: main.ts feeds decodeMappings, which calls decodeVlq, and feeds resolveStack. decodeMappings output and resolveStack go to resolveFrame, then originalPositionFor in lookup.ts, then formatStack.

learning_check.question: Which function decides that a frame is hidden as ignore-listed, and which field does it read?
learning_check.answer: originalPositionFor sets ignored from the map's ignoreList, and formatStack hides every frame where ignored is true.

title: Pick the panel from the reported problem
purpose: Match a reported problem to the one panel that measures it, and see that Lighthouse gathers before it audits.
explanation: A low page score goes to Lighthouse, which gathers a trace and a DevTools log, then audits them into a JSON report (core/runner.js:206-209 @ 3b399f6). Unused bytes go to Coverage. A dark mode bug goes to Rendering, which emulates prefers-color-scheme. A regressed user flow goes to Recorder, which records and replays it.
alt: Decision map: a reported problem branches four ways. Low page score leads to Lighthouse, which gathers then audits into a JSON report; unused bytes lead to Coverage; a dark mode bug leads to Rendering; a regressed flow leads to Recorder. So the symptom picks the panel.

learning_check.question: A report says the checkout flow got slower after the last release. Which panel lets you replay the same flow and measure it again?
learning_check.answer: Recorder. It records a user flow, replays it, and measures it.

title: HAR waterfall report: from file to report
purpose: See how one HAR file becomes three lists: slowest phases, uncached requests and render-blocking candidates.
explanation: The tool parses the HAR text, turns each entry into a request with its seven timing phases, and sends those requests to three small checks. buildReport prints the three answers. The phase values keep -1 as not applicable, so a missing phase is never counted as fast.
alt: Flowchart: checkout.har goes to parseHar, then to toRequests with computePhases, which feeds slowestPhases, isUncached and isRenderBlocking; all three feed buildReport.

learning_check.question: Where does a phase that did not happen, such as DNS on a reused connection, stay out of the results?
learning_check.answer: computePhases keeps it as -1, and slowestPhases and the total skip every value below zero.

title: Trace long task finder: from trace file to report
purpose: Show how a saved Performance trace becomes a list of long tasks and layout shifts.
explanation: main.ts reads the trace file. loadTraceEvents cleans the events. findLongTasks keeps RunTask events longer than 50 ms. findLayoutShifts keeps shifts that did not follow user input. formatReport joins both lists into the printed report.
alt: Flowchart: main.ts reads the trace file, loadTraceEvents parses it, then findLongTasks and findLayoutShifts both read the events, and formatReport prints one report.

learning_check.question: Why do findLongTasks and findLayoutShifts read the output of loadTraceEvents and not the raw file?
learning_check.answer: Reading is separate from judging, so the file is parsed once and both finders get clean events without metadata.
